claim: Cell surface mucins, such as MUC1 and MUC16, are consistently upregulated in epithelial cancers and are considered reliable biomarkers of the disease.
source: Cell surface mucins, such as MUC1 and MUC16, are so consistently upregulated in epithelial cancers that they are considered reliable biomarkers of the disease. (Bast et al., 2009; Rahn et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bast et al., 2009 and Rahn et al., 2001

claim: The ectodomain of cell surface mucins can extend hundreds of nanometers from the plasma membrane.
source: Yet, a striking and defining feature of cell surface mucins is their long, densely glycosylated ectodomain, which can extend hundreds of nanometers from the plasma membrane. (Hattrup and Gendler, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hattrup and Gendler, 2008

claim: Mucins can profoundly enhance the bulk physical properties of the glycocalyx.
source: Consequently, mucins can profoundly enhance the bulk physical properties of the glycocalyx, which is a composite of the polysaccharides and glycoproteins that project from the plasma membrane and decorate all cells.
evidence: Logical inference from the structural properties of mucins described in the text

claim: The bulk physical properties of the glycocalyx can reorganize cell surface receptors such as integrins and alter their activation state.
source: We recently showed that the bulk physical properties of the glycocalyx can exert profound effects on cellular behavior. These effects include a reorganization of cell surface receptors such as integrins. This reorganization alters their activation state and influences not only their ability to interact with extracellular matrix (ECM) ligands but also their synergistic downstream signaling with growth factor receptors. (Paszek et al., 2014; Freeman et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Paszek et al., 2014 and Freeman et al., 2016

claim: An expansive glycocalyx promotes integrin clustering by creating a kinetic funnel where integrins are most likely to bind to the ECM where bonds are already formed.
source: By occluding the majority of binding sites, an expansive glycocalyx paradoxically promotes integrin clustering by creating a kinetic funnel in which integrins are most likely to bind to the ECM where bonds are already formed. (Paszek et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Paszek et al., 2009

claim: Increasing the bulkiness of the glycocalyx enhanced the ability of nonmalignant mammary epithelial cells to grow and survive under minimally adhesive conditions in vitro.
source: In this regard, in vitro studies revealed that increasing the bulkiness of the glycocalyx enhanced the ability of nonmalignant mammary epithelial cells to grow and survive under minimally adhesive conditions whereas otherwise the cells underwent anoikis. (Paszek et al., 2014; Woods et al., 2015; Desgrosellier and Cheresh, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Paszek et al., 2014; Woods et al., 2015; and Desgrosellier and Cheresh, 2010

claim: Tumor aggression is frequently associated with increased expression of mucins which enhance the bulkiness of the glycocalyx.
source: Importantly, we and others have also noted that tumor aggression is frequently associated with an increased expression of mucins which enhance the bulkiness of the glycocalyx and, similarly, that circulating epithelial tumor cells typically express an abundance of mucins. (Paszek et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Paszek et al., 2014

claim: Primary tumor xenografts that overexpress MUC1 grow and metastasize more aggressively.
source: Concomitantly, primary tumor xenografts that overexpress MUC1 grow and metastasize more aggressively (Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015

claim: Mice deficient in MUC1 resist formation of spontaneous tumors.
source: and mice deficient in MUC1 resist formation of spontaneous tumors (Spicer et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spicer et al., 1995

claim: Increasing the thickness of the glycocalyx promotes tumor metastasis by permitting cell cycle progression to facilitate cell proliferation at the metastatic site.
source: Herein, we report that increasing the thickness of the glycocalyx promotes tumor metastasis by permitting cell cycle progression to facilitate cell proliferation at the metastatic site.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the figures

claim: Synthetic glycopolymers with long-term cell surface retention were designed to emulate the structure of mucin ectodomains.
source: We modulated glycocalyx thickness both genetically through ectopic expression of a tailless (signaling defective) MUC1 and more definitively by coating cells with synthetic glycopolymers with long-term cell surface retention that were designed to emulate the structure of mucin ectodomains (Figure 1A). (Woods et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Woods et al., 2015 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: The cholesterylamine lipid confers a long cell surface residence time to glycopolymer conjugates by mediating continuous recycling from an internal reservoir.
source: We previously found that this particular lipid confers a long cell surface residence time to glycopolymer conjugates by mediating continuous recycling from an internal reservoir. (Woods et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Woods et al., 2015

claim: GalNAc-modified poly (MVK) glycopolymers emulate the physical characteristics of native mucins such as length and stiffness.
source: Likewise, GalNAc-modified poly (MVK) glycopolymers emulate the physical characteristics of native mucins such as length and stiffness. (Paszek et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Paszek et al., 2014

claim: GalNAc residues used in the synthetic glycopolymers are considered biochemically inert in mammalian systems.
source: However, unlike the more complex glycans found in native mucins, which can engage in biochemical interactions, (Hudak et al., 2014) the GalNAc residues we used here are considered biochemically inert in mammalian systems.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hudak et al., 2014 and established knowledge

claim: Short glycopolymers are approximately 3 nm in length (degree of polymerization = 36 monomer units).
source: In this work, we used short glycopolymers of ~3 nm in length (degree of polymerization (DP) = 36 monomer units)
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: Long glycopolymers are approximately 90 nm in length (degree of polymerization = 719 monomer units).
source: and long glycopolymers that were ~90 nm in length (DP = 719 monomer units).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: Integrin heterodimer pairs extend roughly 20 nm from the cell membrane.
source: As a point of comparison, integrin heterodimer pairs extend roughly 20 nm from the cell membrane (Figure 1A). (Eng et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Eng et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: Glycopolymers reside on 4TO7 cell surfaces for days.
source: (B) Glycopolymers reside on 4TO7 cell surfaces for days.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B

claim: MCF-10A cells treated with long glycopolymer mucin-mimetics survived longer than those decorated with short glycopolymers when injected into the venous system of nude mice.
source: We found that those cells treated with long glycopolymer mucin-mimetics survived longer, as demonstrated by delayed activation of the apoptosis marker cleaved caspase-3 (CC3), than those decorated with short glycopolymers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: 4TO7 is a Balb/c syngeneic mammary carcinoma that is able to efficiently disseminate and survive for prolonged periods of time at metastatic sites such as the lung.
source: The murine cell line 4TO7 is a Balb/c syngeneic mammary carcinoma that is able to efficiently disseminate and survive for prolonged periods of time at metastatic sites such as the lung. (Aslakson and Miller, 1992)
evidence: Supported by citation to Aslakson and Miller, 1992

claim: 4TO7 cells form predominately dormant tumors because they are unable to proliferate efficiently at the target site.
source: However, the tumor cells in this model form predominately dormant tumors because they are unable to proliferate efficiently at the target site.
evidence: Characterization of the 4TO7 cell line model

claim: By day 13, mice injected with 4TO7 cells coated with long glycopolymers were generating greater photon flux than their counterparts injected with short glycopolymer-treated cells.
source: By day 13, mice injected with 4TO7 cells coated with long glycopolymers were generating greater photon flux, on average, than their counterparts injected with short glycopolymer-treated cells, suggesting a higher density of luciferase-expressing cells and thus an increased tumor burden (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The increase in BLI over time in the long glycopolymer group appeared to approximate an exponential growth-type trend, while the short group did not.
source: In particular, we noted that the increase in BLI over time in the long glycopolymer group appeared to approximate an exponential growth-type trend, while the short group did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: There was no significant difference in accumulation of tumor cells in the lungs between treatment groups as measured by BLI at Day 0.
source: Importantly, we measured no significant difference in accumulation of tumor cells in the lungs between treatment groups as measured by BLI at Day 0.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental observation

claim: Lungs of mice injected with 4TO7 cells endowed with a bulky glycocalyx were significantly heavier than lungs from mice injected with short glycopolymer-bearing cells.
source: We found that the lungs of mice injected with 4TO7 cells endowed with a bulky glycocalyx were significantly heavier than lungs from mice injected with short glycopolymer-bearing cells (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Long glycopolymer-treated 4TO7 cells produced, on average, more than twice the number of metastases per mouse when compared to short glycopolymer-treated cells.
source: Long glycopolymer-treated 4TO7 cells produced, on average, more than twice the number of mets per mouse when compared to short (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1J

claim: Merely increasing the thickness of the glycocalyx was sufficient to increase the metastatic potential of otherwise poorly metastasizing murine carcinoma cells.
source: Thus, merely increasing the thickness of the glycocalyx was sufficient to increase the metastatic potential of otherwise poorly metastasizing murine carcinoma cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data

claim: Short glycopolymers did not increase the metastatic potential of 4TO7 cells when compared to mock (PBS) treated cells.
source: Importantly, the short glycopolymers did not increase the metastatic potential of 4TO7 cells when compared to mock (PBS) treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Metastases from long glycopolymer-treated cells had higher rates of proliferation than those from cells treated with short glycopolymers.
source: Quantitative immunofluorescence (IF) imaging of phosphorylated histone H3 (pH3)—a marker of mitosis—and cleaved caspase-3 (CC3)—a marker of apoptosis—revealed that mets from long glycopolymer-treated cells had higher rates of proliferation than those from cells treated with short glycopolymers (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1K and L

claim: The rates of apoptosis were similar between metastases from long and short glycopolymer-treated cells.
source: But, the rates of apoptosis were similar (Figure 1K and M).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1K and M

claim: Long glycopolymer-painted MCF-10A cells formed colonies with, on average, twice as many cells as colonies formed by short glycopolymer-treated cells or PBS-treated controls on soft PA gels.
source: The long glycopolymer-painted cells formed colonies with, on average, twice as many cells as colonies formed by the short glycopolymer-treated cells or PBS-treated controls (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A–C

claim: The percentage of colonies growing beyond two cells nearly tripled for long-glycopolymer-treated cells versus PBS-treated controls.
source: And the percentage of colonies growing beyond two cells nearly tripled for long-glycopolymer-treated cells verses PBS-treated controls, indicating that this increase in mean colony size was not due merely to a few large colonies (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Cells treated with short-lived but equally long glycopolymers (DPPE) did not produce larger colonies compared to PBS treatment alone.
source: Cells treated with these short-lived but equally long glycopolymers (DPPE) did not produce larger colonies compared to PBS treatment alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The effects of long glycopolymers on colony formation are likely mediated by glycopolymers resident on the cell surface.
source: Thus, the effects measured in Figure 2C and D are likely mediated by glycopolymers resident on the cell surface.
evidence: Inference from the DPPE control experiment

claim: MCF-10A cells plated on stiff PA gels produced higher levels of cyclin D and showed higher levels of pH3 than those on adhesion-poor soft gels.
source: We found that MCF-10A cells plated on stiff PA gels, which offer a rich adhesion setting, produced higher levels of cyclin D (a protein required for cell cycle progression) and showed higher levels of pH3 than those on adhesion-poor soft gels (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: Long glycopolymer-treated cells demonstrated increased cyclin D and pH3 levels, compared to short glycopolymer- and PBS-treated cells, even on soft gels.
source: Long glycopolymer-treated cells also demonstrated increased cyclin D and pH3 levels, compared to short glycopolymer- and PBS-treated cells, even on soft gels, suggesting that a thick glycocalyx drove proliferation and cell cycle progression in this poor adhesion setting.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: A lack of growth factor signaling reduced cyclin D1 and pH3 levels to below the detection limit, even when cells were grown on stiff gels or endowed with a bulky glycocalyx.
source: A lack of growth factor signaling reduced cyclin D1 and pH3 levels to below the detection limit, even when cells were grown on stiff gels or endowed with a bulky glycocalyx (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The underlying drivers of proliferation, including growth factor signaling requirements, appeared to be unaltered by glycocalyx thickness in this model.
source: The underlying drivers of proliferation therefore, including growth factor signaling requirements, appeared to be unaltered by glycocalyx thickness in this model.
evidence: Inference from the serum starvation experiment

claim: A bulky glycocalyx increased Akt phosphorylation on soft gels relative to that in cells with short glycopolymers in MCF-10A cells challenged with EGF.
source: A bulky glycocalyx increased Akt phosphorylation (pAkt), a proxy for activation, on soft gels relative to that in cells with short glycopolymers, while Erk phosphorylation, however, remained unchanged (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2G and H

claim: Erk phosphorylation remained unchanged with a bulky glycocalyx in MCF-10A cells challenged with EGF.
source: A bulky glycocalyx increased Akt phosphorylation (pAkt), a proxy for activation, on soft gels relative to that in cells with short glycopolymers, while Erk phosphorylation, however, remained unchanged (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2G and H

claim: The same effect on pAkt was seen on 4TO7 cells in vitro.
source: The same effect on pAkt was seen on 4TO7 cells in vitro (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2I

claim: IF analysis of tissue sections revealed increased Akt activation in vivo in long glycopolymer-bearing tumor cells when compared to short.
source: As well, IF analysis of tissue sections from the experiments in Figure 1 revealed increased Akt activation, as measured by staining for phosphorylated Akt substrate, in vivo in long glycopolymer-bearing tumor cells when compared to short (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Proliferation of long glycopolymer-painted cells was blocked by an inhibitor of phosphoinositol-3 kinase (PI3K).
source: Consistent with this finding, we repeated the colony formation experiments and found that proliferation of long glycopolymer-painted cells was blocked by an inhibitor of phosphoinositol-3 kinase (PI3K), an upstream activator of Akt, or an inhibitor of MEK—a MAPK downstream of growth factor receptors (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Proliferation of long glycopolymer-painted cells was blocked by an inhibitor of MEK.
source: Consistent with this finding, we repeated the colony formation experiments and found that proliferation of long glycopolymer-painted cells was blocked by an inhibitor of phosphoinositol-3 kinase (PI3K), an upstream activator of Akt, or an inhibitor of MEK—a MAPK downstream of growth factor receptors (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: A bulky glycocalyx drives cell cycle progression via the PI3K-Akt axis.
source: A bulky glycocalyx, therefore, seems to drive cell cycle progression via the PI3K-Akt axis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from inhibitor experiments and phosphorylation data

claim: Metastatic 4TO7 cells in vivo expressed significantly more of the cell cycle progression marker cyclin D1 when bearing long glycopolymers versus short.
source: We were able to confirm the role of glycocalyx-driven cell cycle progression in promoting metastasis in vivo by IF staining of the 4TO7 lung mets from the experiments in Figure 1. Metastatic 4TO7 cells in vivo expressed significantly more of the cell cycle progression marker cyclin D1 when bearing long glycopolymers verses short (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2J and K

claim: Possession of a thick glycocalyx led to enhanced activation of FAK in MCF-10A cells.
source: Western blotting with phospho-specific antibodies revealed that possession of a thick glycocalyx led to enhanced activation of FAK (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: Similar results on FAK activation were seen with 4TO7 cells in vitro.
source: Similar results were seen with 4TO7 cells in vitro (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Cells treated with long glycopolymers along with a nonlethal dose of a specific inhibitor of FAK were unable to form colonies on soft matrices.
source: Reciprocally, cells treated with long glycopolymers along with a nonlethal dose of a specific inhibitor of FAK were unable to form colonies on soft matrices, whereas vehicle (DMSO)-treated, long glycopolymer-coated cells retained colony forming activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Long glycopolymer-treated cells formed tumors with significantly more FAK activation than tumors formed from short glycopolymer-bearing cells in vivo.
source: Long glycopolymer-treated cells formed tumors with significantly more FAK activation than tumors formed from short glycopolymer-bearing cells (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E

claim: A bulky glycocalyx drives integrin clustering through kinetic funneling, leading to increased signaling from focal adhesion-associated proteins such as FAK.
source: A bulky glycocalyx drives integrin clustering through kinetic funneling, leading to increased signaling from focal adhesion-associated proteins such as FAK.
evidence: Model proposed based on experimental data

claim: MUC1ΔCT-expressing 4TO7 cells formed metastases that were growing more rapidly than those formed from MUC1ΔCT-negative cells.
source: BLI photon flux revealed that MUC1ΔCT-expressing cells formed mets that were growing more rapidly than those formed from MUC1ΔCT-negative cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Wet lung mass was nearly doubled in mice injected with MUC1ΔCT-expressing cells versus control.
source: Wet lung mass was nearly doubled in mice injected with MUC1ΔCT-expressing cells versus control (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Nearly three times the number of metastases were formed in the lungs of mice injected with cells expressing the mucin ectodomain compared to those that were not.
source: Nearly three times the number of mets were formed in the lungs of mice injected with cells expressing the mucin ectodomain compared to those that were not (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E

claim: More than twice the number of nuclei in MUC1ΔCT-expressing cells were actively mitotic.
source: pH3 IF staining revealed that more than twice the number of nuclei in MUC1ΔCT-expressing cells were actively mitotic.
evidence: Supported by pH3 staining data

claim: The MUC1 ectodomain increases mechanosignaling, cell cycle progression and MAPK activity in lung metastases.
source: Staining for pY397-FAK, cyclin D1 and pAkt substrate demonstrated that the MUC1 ectodomain increases mechanosignaling, cell cycle progression and MAPK activity in lung mets, further supporting our model (Figure 4I–K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4I–K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: MUC1 is overexpressed in approximately 64% of tumors of all types diagnosed each year in the U.S.
source: MUC1 in particular is overexpressed in ~64% of tumors of all types diagnosed each year in the U.S. (Kufe, 2009b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kufe, 2009b

claim: Ras (K-, H- and N-RAS combined) mutations are estimated to occur in 9–30% of all cancers.
source: As a point of reference, Ras (K-, H- and N-RAS combined) mutations are estimated to occur in 9–30% of all cancers. (Cox et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cox et al., 2014

claim: Hypotheses regarding the mechanism by which MUC1 overexpression drives cancer progression have focused almost entirely on biochemical interactions of its 72-residue cytosolic domain.
source: Hypotheses regarding the mechanism by which MUC1 overexpression drives cancer progression have focused almost entirely on biochemical interactions of its 72-residue cytosolic domain (Kufe, 2009b), which represents <10% of the overall protein sequence.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kufe, 2009b

claim: The cytosolic domain of MUC1 represents less than 10% of the overall protein sequence.
source: Hypotheses regarding the mechanism by which MUC1 overexpression drives cancer progression have focused almost entirely on biochemical interactions of its 72-residue cytosolic domain (Kufe, 2009b), which represents <10% of the overall protein sequence.
evidence: Direct statement based on protein structure

claim: The bulk of MUC1 resides outside the cell where it dominates the physical properties of the glycocalyx.
source: The bulk of MUC1 resides outside the cell where it dominates the physical properties of the glycocalyx.
evidence: Inference from protein structure

claim: The ectodomain of MUC1 profoundly influences focal adhesion formation, integrin signaling, and survival in a minimal adhesion setting.
source: In previous work, we showed that this ectodomain profoundly influences focal adhesion formation, integrin signaling, and survival in a minimal adhesion setting. (Paszek et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Paszek et al., 2014

claim: The model unifies the structure of mucins with their consistent overexpression in metastatic disease.
source: This model unifies the structure of mucins with their consistent overexpression in metastatic disease (Horm and Schroeder, 2013) and the correlation of their overexpression with poor prognosis. (Rahn et al., 2001; Duffy et al., 2000; Retterspitz et al., 2010; McGuckin et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citations to Horm and Schroeder, 2013; Rahn et al., 2001; Duffy et al., 2000; Retterspitz et al., 2010; McGuckin et al., 1995

claim: Drugs targeting the cytoplasmic tail of MUC1 will be missing a key pathophysiologic mechanism.
source: As well, importantly, our results imply that drugs targeting the cytoplasmic tail of MUC1 will be missing a key pathophysiologic mechanism.
evidence: Inference from the study's findings

claim: Sialylated mucin-associated glycans engage the Siglec family of immunomodulatory receptors and may therefore tune the response of critical effector cells in the tumor microenvironment.
source: For example, sialylated mucin-associated glycans engage the Siglec family of immunomodulatory receptors and may therefore tune the response of critical effector cells in the tumor microenvironment. (Belisle et al., 2010; Ohta et al., 2010; Beatson et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Belisle et al., 2010; Ohta et al., 2010; Beatson et al., 2016

claim: Mucins' influence on cancer likely reflects many functional modalities, each contributing differentially to various facets of disease progression.
source: Thus, mucins' influence on cancer likely reflects many functional modalities, each contributing differentially to various facets of disease progression.
evidence: Speculation based on the complexity of mucin functions

claim: Mucins are prime targets for therapeutic intervention and warrant increased focus on avenues for their disruption.
source: From this vantage point, mucins are prime targets for therapeutic intervention and warrant increased focus on avenues for their disruption.
evidence: Speculation based on the study's findings
